title: You don’t have a money problem.
paragraphs: You don’t have a money problem.
You have a worship problem.
Because the question isn’t really, “Should Christians chase wealth or avoid it?”
The real question is: What owns your heart when no one is watching?
You’ve felt it.

That quiet pull when you see someone else succeeding.
That subtle anxiety when your bank account dips.
That internal calculation—If I just had more, I’d finally feel secure.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus never told people to avoid money.
He exposed what money does to you.
And that’s where it gets uncomfortable.

Because you can sit in church, sing worship songs, post Bible verses…
and still be completely mastered by wealth.
You just call it “wisdom,” “planning,” or “providing.”

But God saw it.
You knew.
“No one can serve two masters… You cannot serve God and money.” — Matthew 6:24
Read that again.

Not should not.
Not try not to.
Cannot.
So the issue isn’t possession.
It’s devotion.
Money is not neutral in your heart—it competes.
And it’s patient.

It doesn’t show up screaming, “Worship me.”
It whispers, “Just trust me a little more than God.”
And slowly… you do.

You start making decisions based on income, not obedience.
You measure success by accumulation, not faithfulness.
You hesitate when God calls, because the cost feels too high.
That’s not financial caution.
That’s spiritual compromise.
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil…” — 1 Timothy 6:10
Notice what it doesn’t say.
Money itself isn’t the root.
The love of it is.

That attachment.
That dependence.
That quiet belief that money can do what only God can.

Provide identity.
Give peace.
Secure your future.
But it never delivers.
It just demands more.

More time.
More energy.
More trust.

Until one day, without realizing it…
you’ve built your life around something that cannot save you.
And then Jesus steps in and says something that shocks everyone:
“How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God.” — Luke 18:24
Why?
Because wealth creates a dangerous illusion:
That you don’t need Him.
And that illusion sends people to hell with full bank accounts.
So should Christians chase wealth?
No.
Because chasing wealth means running away from dependence on God.
But should Christians avoid wealth completely?
Also no.
Because God sometimes entrusts resources to His people—not for comfort, but for mission.
“Command those who are rich… not to be arrogant nor to put their hope in wealth… but to put their hope in God… to be rich in good deeds, and to be generous and willing to share.” — 1 Timothy 6:17–18
Do you see it?
The issue isn’t having wealth.
It’s where your hope is.

You can be poor and idolize money.
You can be rich and worship God.
The difference is surrender.
Because the Gospel doesn’t just save your soul—it reorders your priorities.

You stop asking, “How much can I gain?”
And start asking, “How much can I give?”

You stop building your kingdom.
And start investing in His.
Because Jesus didn’t die so you could become financially comfortable.
He died to make you spiritually alive.
“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.” — 2 Corinthians 8:9
That’s the reversal.
He gave up everything.
And we cling to everything.
That’s the tension.
So now you’re standing at a crossroads, whether you admit it or not.
One path looks safe.

Stable income.
Growing savings.
Controlled life.
But God is distant… optional… secondary.
The other path?
It’s riskier.
Not financially—spiritually.
Because it demands trust.

Surrender.
Obedience.
Open hands.
And that terrifies you more than being broke ever could.
So be honest.

If God asked you to give more—would you?
If He asked you to stay when money says leave—would you?
If He asked you to walk away from profit for obedience—would you?
That’s where your answer lives.
Not in what you say.
But in what you choose.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Say it plainly: “God, I choose You over money.”

Not perfectly.
But honestly.
Because silence won’t help them.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—not just inspired, but corrected, sharpened, and discipled—this is where that begins:
Because one day, your bank account won’t matter.
But your soul will.
